population: Finnish men; 43 long-lived healthy vs 92 controls who died at mean age 66.6 (Helsinki Birth Cohort Study), plus 63 healthy men of mean age 83 (Helsinki Businessmen Study)
study_design: case-control, targeted Sanger sequencing of SIRT6 exons
conclusion: T allele carried by 1 of 43 long-lived men versus 9 of 92 earlier-deceased controls; combined two-cohort Fisher exact test gave OR 3.58 (95% CI 0.96-13.4) against longevity for T carriers. Reported power 28%. The paper's abstract states OR 3.53 and p = 0.07 while its Table 2 states 3.58 and 0.074; the table values are recorded here.
provenance_quote: These study findings suggest an inverse association between the T allele of rs117385980 and longevity in Finnish men.

population: Iranian; 227 community-dwelling adults aged 60-90 from the Birjand Longitudinal Aging Study (38 robust, 150 pre-frail, 39 frail)
study_design: cross-sectional case-control, PCR-RFLP with Sanger confirmation
conclusion: Primary frailty analysis was null: T allele frequency 2.13% in non-frail versus 0% in frail (p = 0.36), adjusted OR 0.96. The age gradient is the longevity-relevant result: T allele frequency 1.39% at 60-69, 4.65% at 70-79 and 0% at 80-90 (p = 0.073), directionally consistent with the Finnish cohort. Only 8 heterozygotes were observed in 227 subjects and no homozygote; no mortality follow-up was available.
provenance_quote: a non-significant trend was observed, suggesting a potential inverse relationship between the T allele and advanced age, which may imply a role in longevity
